message.content:
A **CPU (Central Processing Unit)** and a **GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)** are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for drawing images, now also used for highly parallel scientific/ML workloads. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32) optimized for low latency, complex control flow, and large caches. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores optimized for throughput on many identical operations. |
| **Instruction set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) with sophisticated branching, caching, and out‑of‑order execution. | Simpler, often SIMD‑style instructions; each core does the same thing on different data. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, deep pipelines, branch prediction. | Smaller per‑core cache, relies on massive shared memory bandwidth. |
| **Typical workloads** | Single‑threaded or lightly threaded tasks, I/O, system services, database queries. | Data‑parallel tasks: image/video processing, machine‑learning inference/training, scientific simulations. |
| **Performance metric** | FLOPS per core *latency* matters; single‑thread performance is critical. | Throughput matters; millions of floating‑point ops per second across many cores. |
| **Energy efficiency** | Optimized for power‑constrained mobile CPUs, but still high power for high‑end desktop CPUs. | Very efficient at doing the same operation on many data points; great for compute‑heavy, parallelizable work. |

In short, a CPU excels at diverse, sequential tasks with complex logic, while a GPU shines when you can break a problem into many identical, independent sub‑tasks that can run simultaneously. This makes GPUs ideal for rendering graphics and accelerating workloads like deep learning, whereas CPUs remain essential for general operating‑system and application logic.
